title: Woman's death no surprise to friends; Victim had tough life with gender identity
article: Chevranna Abdi's death in police custody came as a sad shock to a handful of friends in the gay and transgendered communities who had been searching for her for several months.
But it was not a surprise.

Abdi, who told people she was 26, collapsed after being arrested in a disturbance at a Sanford Avenue North apartment she was visiting Thursday night and was pronounced dead a short time later at Hamilton General Hospital.

Residents of the apartment building called police about a woman running through the halls threatening others with a large knife. The building superintendent and an assistant disarmed a woman and held her for police on the eighth floor.

Ontario's Special Investigations Unit -- the civilian agency that investigates incidents involving police and civilians that have resulted in serious injury, sexual assault or death -- yesterday designated three Hamilton police officers as subject officers in their probe of Abdi's death.
That means their conduct may have caused the circumstances under investigation.
Four officers have already been designated as witnesses.
Abdi was born Abdirhaman Abdi, about 30 years ago. He was the only boy in a devout Muslim family with seven girls.
Abdi will be buried this afternoon following a funeral at the Hamilton Mosque on Stone Church Road East.
David Petrovic, who met Abdi at Sir John A. Macdonald high school 12 years ago, said his friend began to self-identify and live as a woman 10 years ago.

He knew she had been living in Toronto and saw her regularly as a friend when she would come to Hamilton. He was able to congratulate her when she took first prize in the Miss New York Continental Pageant, one of a series of "classy beauty pageants for drag performers" in 1999.
Chevranna was the name Abdi used on stage.
Petrovic said his friend was torn between her love for her family and living as normal a life as was possible given her change of lifestyle.
"Her mom is Somalian, her dad is from Saudi Arabia," Petrovic said.
And, he noted, there was a lot more distance between Chevranna and her parents than the mileage from Hamilton to their home in Atlanta, Ga.
Petrovic believes the disturbance Thursday night was fuelled by drugs.
He had seen his friend "out of control" on drugs before. He'd been on the receiving end of her temper in the past, ducking beer bottles hurled at his head.
"The drugs were so senseless and useless," he said.

Petrovic heard last summer that Abdi was in Hamilton but he could not find her. In the past four or five months, he took to walking popular sex trade strolls, showing her picture and asking if anyone had seen his friend.
"For whatever reasons, she did not want to be found."
In the end, he said, Abdi had been living "a pretty harsh life" the past year or two.
"I am sure she was on something (Thursday) night. I have been around long enough to know when someone is out of control.
"Deep down, she was a good person who helped other people in the transgendered community who weren't sure where they were at."
Petrovic's and Chevranna's transgendered Toronto friend Tatianna Adams said Abdi was terrified to be alone.
"She would do anything to have her friends come and stay with her if she thought she would be alone," said Petrovic.
He said the last he heard of Abdi was a message she left on his phone on Valentine's Day asking for company. She did not say where she was.
Adams said Abdi's fear of being alone or an outsider exacerbated the feelings she already had as an immigrant child and compounded the strain of being estranged from her family.
The thing Abdi wanted most -- reconciliation with her family, especially her father -- eluded her.
"She wanted that more than anything else in the world," Adams said.
But it meant giving up "who she was," Petrovic added
In the end, Adams said, Abdi "felt what (transgendered persons) feel, being all alone in a crowd of a thousand.
"She loved to come to my parents' house and they made a fuss over her but it made her feel more like an outsider because she didn't have that herself."

Essentially, a transgendered person is someone whose core gender identity does not coincide with their biological organs. Transgendered people include transsexuals, cross-dressers and those whose gender roles are ambiguous.
The term is a relatively new one, meant to clarify that gender is the issue rather than sexual orientation.
Adams estimated there may be "a couple hundred" transgendered people living in the Hamilton area.
It is generally thought 2 per cent of the general population may be transgendered but they can be difficult to find, remaining invisible in a society organized according to fixed gender.
